title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Condensed
subtitle: Agents, search, logic, probability, learning and more, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A condensed course based on the structure of Russell and Norvig's Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th edition), written in original words: rational agents, search and games, constraint satisfaction, logic and planning, probability and Bayesian networks, temporal models, decisions and MDPs, game theory, machine learning, neural networks and reinforcement learning, and applications and ethics. Theory plus Python labs.

chapters.title: What AI is: rational agents

maps.title: Agents
links: Learning agent | improves | Its performance element

summary: Artificial intelligence is the study of building agents: things that perceive an environment and act in it. This course follows the structure of the textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach by Russell and Norvig, condensed and re-explained in original words.
The central idea is the rational agent. It picks the action that is expected to give the best score on a performance measure, given what it has perceived so far.
Rationality is not perfection. The agent cannot know what it could not perceive. It is judged on expected, not lucky, outcomes.

glossary.def: Anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts through actuators.
Everything the agent has perceived so far.
An agent that chooses the action with the best expected performance.
The score that says how well the environment is doing.
Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
The sensors give the whole relevant state.

keyPoints: An agent maps percept sequences to actions.
Rational means best expected performance, not omniscient.
Describe a task with PEAS before designing the agent.
Environments differ: observable or not, deterministic or not, episodic or sequential, static or dynamic.
Agent types: simple reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning.
The standard model: optimise a fixed objective. Its danger is a wrong objective.

items: ELI5. An AI agent is like a thermostat with ambition: it senses the room, decides, and acts. A rational one picks whatever should work best on average, even though it cannot see everything.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what makes an agent rational, and why is that not the same as perfect?
Early definitions of AI argued about whether a machine should think like a human or act like one, and whether it should be judged by human behaviour or by an ideal standard.
The approach that won out in practice is to define AI by what an agent does: it should act to achieve its goals as well as it can.

An agent is a function from everything it has perceived to an action. A table listing an action for every possible history would be astronomically large, so real agents are programs that compute the action compactly.

Consider a vacuum cleaner agent in two rooms. Its sensors tell it which room it is in and whether that room is dirty. Its actuators let it move left, move right or suck. A sensible performance measure awards one point per clean room per time step.
Notice the measure is about the world, not about how the agent feels.

Task environments are described by PEAS. For an automated taxi: the performance measure covers safety, speed, comfort and cost; the environment is roads, traffic and pedestrians; the actuators are steering, brakes and horn; the sensors are cameras, radar and GPS.

Five agent designs grow in power. A simple reflex agent reacts to the current percept with condition-action rules. A model-based agent keeps an internal picture of the world. A goal-based agent searches for actions that reach a goal. A utility-based agent weighs trade-offs with a numeric utility.
A learning agent improves any of these from experience.

Modern AI mostly follows the standard model: build a machine that optimises an objective we give it. This works only if the objective is right. A very capable machine with a slightly wrong objective can do real harm, which is why later chapters return to uncertainty about objectives and to ethics.

quiz.q: Which describes a rational agent?
options: It maximises expected performance given what it perceived
It always makes the perfect move

quiz.q: What does PEAS stand for?

chapters.title: Solving problems by search

maps.title: Search
links: Breadth-first | finds | Shortest path in steps

summary: A problem-solving agent looks ahead. It models the world as states and actions, then searches for a sequence of actions leading to a goal.

Uninformed methods use only the problem definition: breadth-first, uniform-cost, depth-first and iterative deepening. Informed methods use a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. A star search combines the cost so far with that estimate and is optimal when the estimate never overestimates.
The labs write breadth-first search and A star on a small graph.

glossary.def: All states reachable from the start by any actions.
Nodes that are generated but not yet expanded.
An estimate h(n) of the cost from n to the goal.
A heuristic that never overestimates the true cost.
The number of successors per state, b.
A search that always finds a cheapest solution.

keyPoints: Define a problem by initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path cost.
BFS is complete and finds the fewest steps, but uses O(b^d) memory.
Uniform-cost search expands the cheapest frontier node first.
Depth-first uses little memory but may not find the best path.
A* orders by f = g + h; optimal if h is admissible (and consistent for graph search).
Heuristics come from relaxed problems.

items: ELI5. Search is exploring a maze with a pencil. Breadth-first checks every nearby corridor first; A-star also guesses how far the exit is, so it wastes fewer steps.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why must the guess never be too big for A-star to stay correct?

Imagine finding a route from one city to another. A state is a city, an action is a road, and a goal is reaching the destination. The set of all cities and roads forms a graph. Search explores this graph from the start, keeping a frontier of places it has seen but not yet explored.

Breadth-first search expands the oldest frontier node first, using a queue. It finds the path with the fewest steps. Its drawback is memory: the frontier can hold every node at the current depth, which grows like b to the power d.

Roads have different lengths. Uniform-cost search expands the node with the lowest cost so far, using a priority queue. It finds the cheapest path. Depth-first search uses a stack and little memory, but can wander down a long path and miss shorter ones.
Informed search adds knowledge. A heuristic h(n) estimates the remaining cost. For a map, the straight-line distance to the goal is a good one: no road is shorter than a straight line.

A star expands the node with the smallest f, where g is the cost so far and h the estimate of the cost to go. If h never overestimates, A star is optimal. If h is also consistent, meaning h(n) is at most the step cost plus h of the next node, it never needs to reopen a node.

Where do heuristics come from? Often from a relaxed version of the problem. In the sliding tile puzzle, pretend tiles can pass through each other; the number of moves needed is the sum of tile distances, the Manhattan distance, which is admissible.

quiz.q: Which search finds the path with fewest steps?
What does an admissible heuristic do?
What does A* sort the frontier by?

cards.a: It stores a whole level of nodes.

practice.title: A* loop
practice.intro: Put the A* steps in order.

Remove the node with the lowest f

chapters.title: Beyond classical search: local search and games

maps.title: Local search and games
links: Hill climbing | moves to | Best neighbour
Simulated annealing | accepts | Some worse moves
Monte Carlo tree search | uses | Random playouts

summary: Some problems have no meaningful path, only a good final state. Local search keeps a single state and improves it step by step. Hill climbing can get stuck on a local maximum; random restarts and simulated annealing help.

In two-player games, minimax chooses the move that is best assuming the opponent also plays best. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the decision. Monte Carlo tree search, used in Go programs, chooses moves by many random playouts.
The labs compute a minimax value and a hill climb.

glossary.def: Search that keeps only the current state.
Repeatedly move to the best neighbour.
Hill climbing that sometimes accepts worse moves, less often over time.
Best move assuming optimal play by both sides.
Skipping branches that cannot matter.
An estimate of a position's value.

keyPoints: Local search uses little memory and suits optimisation.
Hill climbing: local maxima, ridges and plateaus.
Simulated annealing accepts a worse move with probability exp(delta/T).
Minimax value: max at our turns, min at the opponent's.
Alpha-beta can double the reachable depth with good move ordering.
MCTS balances exploring and exploiting with random rollouts.

items: ELI5. Hill climbing is climbing in fog: you always step up, and may end on a small hill. In games you plan by imagining your opponent always plays their very best reply.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what can trap hill climbing, and how does minimax think about the opponent?

Think of climbing a hill in fog: you can only see nearby ground. Hill climbing moves to the best neighbouring state and stops when none is better. It is fast, but can stop on a small hill that is not the highest one.

Two cures are popular. Random restarts run hill climbing many times from different starting points. Simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse move, with a probability that shrinks as a temperature value falls. Early on it explores widely; later it settles.
Games add an opponent. Minimax searches the game tree. At our moves we take the maximum value, at the opponent's moves the minimum. The value of the root is what we get if both sides play perfectly.

Games are big, so we cut off the search at some depth and use an evaluation function to score the position. Alpha-beta pruning keeps a window of values already guaranteed to each side and stops exploring a branch once it cannot beat them. The result is the same as minimax but with far fewer nodes.

Monte Carlo tree search suits games like Go, where evaluation by hand is hard. It repeats four steps: select a promising node, expand it, play a random game to the end, and back up the result. Nodes that win more often get visited more.
Games with chance, such as backgammon, add chance nodes with expected values. Games with hidden information, such as poker, need reasoning about belief states.

chapters.title: Constraint satisfaction

maps.title: CSP
links: Constraint graph | shows | Which variables interact
Backtracking | assigns | One variable at a time

summary: A constraint satisfaction problem, or CSP, is defined by variables, the values each may take, and constraints on which combinations are allowed. Map colouring, scheduling and Sudoku are classic examples.

Because constraints expose structure, a CSP solver can do much better than blind search. Backtracking assigns variables one at a time and undoes a choice when a constraint fails. Propagation, such as forward checking and arc consistency, removes impossible values early.
The labs write a constraint check and a backtracking colour solver.

glossary.def: A thing to assign a value to.
The set of allowed values for a variable.
A restriction on combinations of values.
Every value has a supporting value in each neighbour.
Choose the variable with the fewest remaining values.
Local search that reassigns a conflicted variable.

keyPoints: CSP = variables + domains + constraints.
Backtracking is depth-first search over partial assignments.
Forward checking removes values that a new assignment rules out.
Arc consistency propagates constraints between variable pairs.
Order heuristics: MRV, degree, least-constraining value.
A tree-shaped constraint graph can be solved in linear time.

items: ELI5. Colouring a map is a puzzle with rules. Instead of trying everything, you cross off colours that can no longer work and go back as soon as you hit a dead end.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how does crossing off options early save work?

Colouring a map so that neighbouring regions differ is a classic CSP. The variables are the regions, the domain of each is the set of colours, and the constraints say neighbours must differ. A solution is a complete assignment that breaks no constraint.

Plain search would try combinations without noticing that a bad choice early on dooms everything after it. Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and as soon as a constraint is violated it goes back and tries a different value.

Constraint propagation makes this far stronger. Forward checking, after each assignment, removes from the neighbours' domains any value that now conflicts. If a domain empties, we back up at once. Arc consistency goes further: a value is removed if some neighbour has no value compatible with it.

Heuristics for choosing matter a lot. Minimum remaining values picks the variable with the fewest legal values, so failures show up early. The degree heuristic breaks ties by choosing the variable involved in the most constraints.
The least-constraining value rule tries the value that rules out the fewest options for neighbours.

For some problems local search works better. Min-conflicts starts from a full assignment, picks a conflicted variable and gives it the value that causes the fewest conflicts. It solves huge problems such as n-queens remarkably fast.
Structure helps. If the constraint graph is a tree, the problem can be solved in time linear in the number of variables. Otherwise we can cut the graph into a tree by assigning a few variables first.

What does MRV choose?
options: The variable with the fewest legal values

quiz.q: When can a CSP be solved in linear time?
options: When the constraint graph is a tree

cards.a: Variables as nodes, constraints as edges.

chapters.title: Logical agents: propositional logic

maps.title: Logic
links: Entailment | means | True in all models

summary: A knowledge-based agent keeps sentences in a knowledge base and uses inference to decide what to do. Propositional logic has symbols that are true or false, combined with not, and, or, implies and if and only if.

A sentence is entailed by the knowledge base if it is true in every model where the knowledge base is true. Inference algorithms are sound if they derive only entailed sentences and complete if they derive all of them. Resolution is sound and complete for propositional logic.
The labs evaluate sentences and test entailment by enumerating models.

glossary.def: A set of sentences held true.
An assignment of true or false to every symbol.
KB entails a when a holds in every model of KB.
Derives only what is entailed.
Can derive everything that is entailed.
A clause with at most one positive literal.

keyPoints: Syntax defines sentences; semantics defines their truth in a model.
Entailment: KB entails a iff KB and not a is unsatisfiable.
Model checking is exponential in the number of symbols.
Resolution proves entailment by deriving the empty clause.
Horn clauses admit forward and backward chaining in linear time.
Modern SAT solvers handle millions of clauses (DPLL, clause learning).

items: ELI5. Logic is a rulebook for certainty. If the rules say a thing must be true in every possible world that fits the facts, then it follows. Checking all worlds works, but gets huge fast.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does it mean for one sentence to follow from others?

A knowledge-based agent tells its knowledge base what it perceives and asks what to do. The strength of this design is that the knowledge is stated declaratively, and the same inference engine works on many problems.

In propositional logic a symbol such as Rain is either true or false. A model assigns a value to every symbol. We combine symbols with not, and, or, implies and if and only if. A sentence is true or false in each model by simple rules.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} KB \models \alpha \\[0.6em] \Longleftrightarrow \\[0.6em] \text{every model of } KB \text{ is a model of } \alpha \end{gathered}

items: The simplest inference is model checking: enumerate all assignments and check that alpha is true wherever the knowledge base is true. It is sound and complete, but with n symbols there are 2 to the n models.

Resolution works on clauses, which are disjunctions of literals. From two clauses that contain a complementary pair, it derives a new clause without that pair. To prove alpha, add not alpha to the knowledge base and try to derive the empty clause, which signals a contradiction.

If the knowledge base consists of Horn clauses, inference is simpler. Forward chaining fires rules whose premises are known until the query appears. Backward chaining works from the goal. Both run in time linear in the size of the knowledge base.

The Wumpus world is a small cave game used to show these ideas. Pits cause breezes in adjacent squares; the Wumpus causes a stench. By combining percepts with rules, the agent can prove which squares are safe.

quiz.q: What does KB entails a mean?
options: a is true in every model where KB is true

quiz.q: Which inference method is sound and complete for propositional logic?
Why are Horn clauses attractive?

chapters.title: First-order logic and inference

maps.title: FOL
links: First-order logic | adds | Objects and relations
Quantifiers | are | For all and there exists

summary: Propositional logic cannot say that all humans are mortal without listing every human. First-order logic adds objects, relations, functions and quantifiers, so general facts are stated once.
Inference uses unification: finding a substitution that makes two expressions identical. With unification, rules can be chained forward or backward, and resolution works on clauses with variables.
The labs write a small unifier and a term matcher.

glossary.def: A relation over objects, such as Brother(x, y).
For all (∀) or there exists (∃).
An expression that names an object.
A substitution that makes two expressions the same.
A new name that stands for an existential witness.
A structured vocabulary of categories and relations.

keyPoints: Use implies with for-all and and with there-exists.
Not-for-all x P is the same as there-exists x not P.
Unification finds the most general substitution.
The occur check stops a variable from binding to a term containing it.
FOL entailment is semi-decidable.
Prolog uses backward chaining on Horn clauses.

items: ELI5. Variables in logic are blanks like 'someone'. Matching a rule to a fact is like fitting a puzzle piece: you fill the blanks the same way on both sides.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does unification do with the blanks?

First-order logic talks about objects and the relations between them. Constants name objects, predicates state relations, and functions map objects to objects. With the quantifier for-all and there-exists we make general claims.

A common mistake is the wrong connective. For all x, if Human of x then Mortal of x uses implies. Writing and would claim that everything is human and mortal. For there-exists we use and: some x is human and happy.

To reason, we need to match general rules against specific facts. Unification does this. To unify Knows(John, x) with Knows(y, Mary), we bind y to John and x to Mary. The result is the most general unifier: it commits to as little as needed.

Forward chaining applies rules to facts to derive new facts until a goal appears. Backward chaining works from the goal, finding rules whose conclusion matches and treating their premises as sub-goals. Prolog is built on backward chaining.

Resolution extends to first-order logic by converting sentences to clauses: remove implications, move negations inward, replace existentials by Skolem constants or functions, drop universal quantifiers. Then resolve clauses that unify. It is refutation-complete.

Building a knowledge base is knowledge engineering. Decide the vocabulary, encode general axioms, add the specific problem, and test by asking queries. Large shared vocabularies, called ontologies, organise categories such as events, time and substances.

quiz.q: What does unification produce?

chapters.title: Planning and knowledge representation

maps.title: Planning
links: Precondition | must hold | Before an action

summary: Classical planning finds a sequence of actions that turns an initial state into a goal in a deterministic, fully observable world. States are sets of facts. Each action has preconditions and effects that add and delete facts.

A planner can search forward from the start, backward from the goal, or use heuristics from relaxed problems. Hierarchical task networks plan with high-level tasks refined into primitive steps, and are the practical choice in many applications.
Knowledge representation organises the world into categories with inheritance, and supports default reasoning that can be withdrawn.

glossary.def: An atomic statement that is true in a state.
Facts that must hold for an action to apply.
Facts added and deleted by an action.
A standard language for describing planning problems.
Hierarchical task network planning.
Concluding something unless told otherwise.

keyPoints: A planning problem = initial state, actions, goal.
An action applies if its preconditions are a subset of the state.
Applying: remove the delete list, add the add list.
Forward search is simple; heuristics make it practical.
The delete-relaxation ignores deletions to estimate distance.
Nonmonotonic reasoning lets conclusions be withdrawn.

items: ELI5. A plan is a recipe: each step needs some things in place and changes the kitchen. Planning is finding the recipe that goes from where you are to the dish you want.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what do preconditions and effects mean for one step?

Planning is search with structure. Instead of an opaque state, the state is a set of facts, such as At(Robot, Kitchen) and Holding(Cup). Each action lists what must be true to do it and what it changes.

Take the action Move from X to Y. Its precondition is At(X). Its effect adds At(Y) and deletes At(X). To check whether an action applies, test that its preconditions are all in the state. To apply it, remove the deleted facts and add the new ones.

With this representation a forward planner searches from the initial state by trying every applicable action. A backward planner starts at the goal and finds actions that could have produced it. Both can use A star with a heuristic.

A good heuristic comes from relaxation. Pretend actions never delete anything. Then each action only helps, and the number of steps to reach the goal in the relaxed problem is a lower bound on the real number. Modern planners are built on such heuristics.

Real tasks are better organised hierarchically. To travel, first book, then go to the airport, then fly. A hierarchical task network stores such recipes and refines abstract tasks into concrete steps. The designer's knowledge shrinks the search.

Knowledge representation also asks how to organise categories. Objects belong to categories, categories form hierarchies and properties are inherited. Defaults such as birds fly are useful even though penguins are exceptions, so reasoning must be able to withdraw a conclusion.

quiz.q: When does an action apply?
options: When its preconditions are in the state
When its effects are in the state

quiz.q: What does the delete relaxation ignore?

chapters.title: Uncertainty: probability and Bayes' rule

maps.title: Probability
links: Conditional probability | updates | Belief given evidence

summary: An agent rarely knows the whole truth. Probability theory gives it a language for degrees of belief. Combined with utility it yields decision theory.

From a full joint distribution any query can be answered by summing matching entries and dividing. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional: it turns the chance of symptoms given a disease into the chance of the disease given symptoms.
The labs compute posteriors and a naive Bayes score.

glossary.def: Belief before seeing evidence.
Belief after seeing evidence.
P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b).
Knowing one tells nothing about the other.
P(evidence | hypothesis).
How common the hypothesis is overall.

keyPoints: Probabilities lie in 0..1 and sum to 1 over possible worlds.
P(a or b) = P(a) + P(b) - P(a and b).
Bayes: P(h | e) = P(e | h) P(h) / P(e).
Ignoring the base rate causes many errors.
Full joint tables grow as 2^n.
Naive Bayes: P(cause, e1..en) = P(cause) times the product of P(ei | cause).

items: ELI5. Probability is honest guessing with numbers. A rare disease and a good-but-imperfect test: most positives are false alarms because so few people are ill to begin with.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is a positive result on a rare disease usually still unlikely to be real?
Logic fails when we are not sure. A patient with a toothache may have a cavity, or gum disease, or something else. Probability expresses how likely each is, given what we know.

The full joint distribution lists the probability of every combination of values. Given it, we can answer any question. To find the probability of a cavity given a toothache, sum the entries with both and divide by the sum of entries with a toothache.

This is Bayes' rule. It is useful because diagnostic knowledge, the chance of a disease given symptoms, is hard to collect, while causal knowledge, the chance of symptoms given the disease, is easier and more stable.

Here is a worked case. A disease affects 1 person in 10,000. A test catches it 99 percent of the time but gives a false alarm 1 percent of the time. If you test positive, the chance you are ill is about 1 percent. In 10,000 people there is one true positive and about 100 false positives.
The base rate dominates.

Full joint tables are too large, so we use independence. Naive Bayes assumes the effects are independent given the cause, so the joint is the prior times a product of simple likelihoods. It is crude, but works well for tasks like spam filtering.

quiz.q: What does Bayes' rule give?

chapters.title: Bayesian networks

maps.title: Bayes nets
links: Bayesian network | is | A directed acyclic graph

summary: A Bayesian network shows how variables depend on one another. Each node is a variable with a table giving its probability conditioned on its parents. The network represents the full joint compactly as a product of those local tables.
To answer a query, sum over the hidden variables. Variable elimination does this efficiently. For networks that are too large, sampling methods approximate the answer.
The labs compute a joint probability and answer a query by enumeration.

glossary.def: A random variable.
Conditional probability table for a node given its parents.
A node with an arrow into another.
A variable that is neither evidence nor the query.
Parents, children and the children's other parents.
Evidence for one cause lowers belief in another.

keyPoints: The joint is the product of P(X | parents(X)).
A network with n Boolean nodes and at most k parents needs n times 2^k numbers.
Enumeration sums the joint over hidden variables.
A node is independent of non-descendants given its parents.
Exact inference is hard in general; easy on trees.
Likelihood weighting and Gibbs sampling approximate.

items: ELI5. A Bayesian network is a map of what causes what, with a small table at each place. Together the tables answer questions like: the alarm rang, was it a burglar?
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is explaining away?

Imagine a burglar alarm. A burglary or an earthquake may set it off. If it rings, either neighbour may call you. A Bayesian network draws arrows from burglary and earthquake to alarm, and from alarm to each call.
Each node stores a table. Burglary has a small prior. The alarm's table gives its chance of ringing for each combination of burglary and earthquake. A call's table depends only on the alarm.

To find the chance of a burglary given that both neighbours called, enumerate: sum the joint over every value of the hidden variables (earthquake and alarm), then normalise across burglary or no burglary.

The network also shows independence. If you already know the alarm state, the calls tell you nothing more about the burglary. And when the alarm is observed, burglary and earthquake become competing explanations: hearing about an earthquake makes a burglary less likely. This is explaining away.
Variable elimination avoids repeating work by storing intermediate tables and summing out variables one at a time.

When exact inference is too costly, approximate methods draw samples: likelihood weighting fixes the evidence and weights each sample, and Gibbs sampling walks through states by resampling one variable at a time.

quiz.q: How does a Bayes net define the joint?
options: Product of each node given its parents

quiz.q: What is explaining away?
options: A cause becomes less likely when another is confirmed

chapters.title: Reasoning over time
summary: Worlds change, and an agent must track hidden state over time from noisy observations. Temporal models assume the state depends on a bounded past (the Markov assumption) and each observation depends only on the current state.

Filtering computes the belief about the present from all evidence so far, and can be updated recursively in constant time per step. Hidden Markov models, Kalman filters and particle filters are the main tools.
The labs write one step of a prediction and a filtering update.

glossary.def: What we want to know but cannot see.
P(next state | current state).
P(observation | state).
Estimating the current state from all evidence.
Hidden Markov model with one discrete state variable.
Filtering by tracking weighted samples.

keyPoints: Markov assumption: the present depends on a bounded past.
Sensor assumption: observation depends on the current state only.
Filtering update: predict, then weight by the evidence, then normalise.
Smoothing uses future evidence to improve past estimates.
Kalman filters: linear dynamics with Gaussian noise.
Particle filters: propagate, weight, resample.

items: ELI5. Tracking something hidden over time is like guessing the weather from umbrellas. Each day you predict, then adjust your guess by what you actually saw.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the predict and update steps?

A guard in a windowless room wants to know whether it is raining outside. The only clue each day is whether the visitor carries an umbrella. The weather is a hidden state that changes slowly; the umbrella is a noisy observation.

A model needs two tables. The transition model says how likely tomorrow's weather is, given today's. The sensor model says how likely an umbrella is, given the weather. With the Markov assumption, tomorrow depends on today only, not on the whole past.

lesson.tex: P(X_{t+1}\mid e_{1:t+1}) \;\propto\; P(e_{t+1}\mid X_{t+1}) \sum_{x_t} P(X_{t+1}\mid x_t)\,P(x_t\mid e_{1:t})

items: This is the filtering update. First predict: push the current belief through the transition model. Then update: multiply by how well each state explains the new observation, and normalise. The cost per step does not grow with time, so an agent can filter forever.

Other tasks use the same machinery. Prediction runs the transition model forward with no new evidence. Smoothing improves an estimate of the past using later evidence. The most likely sequence, found by the Viterbi algorithm, is used in speech recognition.

When the state is continuous, a Kalman filter keeps a Gaussian belief and is exact for linear dynamics. For nonlinear or multimodal problems, a particle filter keeps many samples: it moves each, weights it by the evidence, and resamples. Robots use particle filters to locate themselves on maps.

practice.title: Predict step
practice.intro: Write predict(belief, trans): belief is a list of probabilities over states; trans[i][j] = P(next = j | current = i). Return the predicted belief list, each rounded to 9 decimals.

practice.title: Filter step
practice.intro: Write filter_step(belief, trans, sensor, obs): sensor[j][o] = P(observation o | state j); obs is the observed index. Predict with trans, weight by the observation, normalise; return the new belief, each rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.solution:
def filter_step(belief, trans, sensor, obs):
    n = len(belief)
    pred = []
    for j in range(n):
        s = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            s += belief[i] * trans[i][j]
        pred.append(s)
    w = [pred[j] * sensor[j][obs] for j in range(n)]
    tot = sum(w)
    return [round(x / tot, 9) for x in w]

chapters.title: Making decisions: utility and MDPs

maps.title: Decisions
links: Risk aversion | bends | Utility of money

summary: A rational agent chooses the action with the highest expected utility: the sum over outcomes of probability times utility. Utility of money is usually concave, which explains risk aversion.

When decisions come in sequence, we use a Markov decision process: states, actions, a transition model and rewards. The solution is a policy that gives an action for each state. Value iteration computes it by repeatedly applying the Bellman update.
The labs write expected utility and value iteration.

glossary.def: A number that says how much an outcome is preferred.
Probability-weighted average of utilities.
Markov decision process.
A rule that gives an action for each state.
Gamma below one: how much future rewards count.
U(s) = R(s) + gamma max over a of sum P(s' | s, a) U(s').

keyPoints: Maximise expected utility.
A concave utility of money means risk aversion.
A policy, not a plan, is the solution when outcomes are uncertain.
Value iteration repeats the Bellman update until values settle.
Policy iteration alternates evaluating and improving a policy.
A POMDP is an MDP with hidden state: plan over belief states.

items: ELI5. A decision under uncertainty weighs each outcome by how likely and how good it is. A series of decisions needs a rule for every situation: a policy, not a single plan.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is a policy needed instead of a plan?

Suppose you can take a sure 40 dollars or a coin flip that pays 100 or nothing. The coin flip has an expected value of 50, yet many people take the sure 40. That is not irrational: the tenth extra dollar is worth less than the first. Utility captures this: it is a curve, not a straight line.
The principle of maximum expected utility says to pick the action with the largest value of this sum. It follows from a few reasonable axioms about preferences, such as transitivity.
People do violate the axioms in practice, as the Allais paradox shows, but the principle remains the design standard for machines.

Many problems need a sequence of decisions in an uncertain world. A Markov decision process has states, actions, a transition model P(s' | s, a), and a reward per state. Because outcomes are uncertain, the answer is a policy: what to do in every state we might reach.

This is the Bellman equation. The utility of a state is its reward plus the discounted expected utility of the best action. Value iteration starts with all utilities at zero and applies the equation to every state again and again.
It converges because the update shrinks differences by the factor gamma. The best policy then picks the action that achieves the maximum.

cards.a: Preferring a sure payoff over a gamble.

chapters.title: Multiple agents and game theory

maps.title: Game theory
links: Nash equilibrium | is | No profitable deviation

summary: When several agents act, each one's best choice depends on the others. Game theory studies this. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no player gains by changing alone.

The prisoner's dilemma shows that individually rational choices can leave everyone worse off. Mechanism design flips the question: choose the rules so that self-interested agents produce a good result. A Vickrey auction makes honest bidding the best strategy.
The labs find equilibria and run an auction.

glossary.def: A rule for choosing actions.
What a player receives from an outcome.
Best whatever others do.
No player can gain by changing alone.
The rules of an interaction.
Highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.

keyPoints: Normal form: a table of payoffs.
Dominant strategies are the simplest solution.
Not every game has a pure Nash equilibrium; mixed strategies always exist.
In the prisoner's dilemma defection is dominant, yet cooperation pays more.
Vickrey: bidding your true value is dominant.
Social choice: Arrow's theorem limits fair voting.

items: ELI5. A game is a situation where my best move depends on yours. In the prisoner's dilemma, each does best by betraying, yet both would be better off trusting. Rule design can fix this.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is a Nash equilibrium in plain words?

In a game, a player's payoff depends on everyone's choices. Take two suspects held apart. If both stay silent they get a light sentence. If one confesses while the other stays silent, the confessor goes free. If both confess, both get a medium sentence.

Whatever the other does, confessing is better for you. It is a dominant strategy. So both confess, and both get the medium sentence, although mutual silence would have been better for both. Individual rationality leads to a collective loss.

A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies such that no player can do better by changing their own strategy while the others stay put. In the prisoner's dilemma, both confessing is the unique equilibrium.
Some games, like rock-paper-scissors, have no equilibrium in pure strategies, only in mixed ones where players randomise.
Repeating the game changes the picture. When players meet many times, strategies such as tit-for-tat, which cooperates first and then copies the other's last move, can sustain cooperation.
Mechanism design is game theory in reverse: pick the rules to get the outcome you want. In a sealed-bid second-price auction, the winner pays the second-highest bid.
Then bidding anything other than your true value cannot help you: a lower bid risks losing a profitable win, a higher bid risks winning at a loss. Truth telling is a dominant strategy.

When people vote, the picture is hard. Arrow's theorem shows that no ranked voting rule satisfies a short list of fairness conditions at the same time. The best we can do is choose which compromises to accept.

chapters.title: Learning from examples

maps.title: Learning
links: Supervised learning | maps | Inputs to outputs
Decision tree | splits on | Information gain

summary: Learning lets an agent improve from data. In supervised learning the data are input-output pairs and the aim is a function that predicts well on new inputs. The main danger is overfitting: a model that fits noise in the training data.

Decision trees split on the attribute with the highest information gain. Linear models fit a line or plane by minimising squared error, using a formula or gradient descent. Nearest neighbours predict from the closest examples. Ensembles such as random forests combine many models.
The labs compute entropy, nearest neighbours and a gradient step.

glossary.def: Examples used to fit the model.
Held-out examples used to estimate performance.
Low training error but high error on new data.
A measure of uncertainty in a distribution.
Reduction in entropy from a split.
A penalty that discourages complex models.

keyPoints: Hold out data to measure generalisation.
Bias-variance trade-off: simple models underfit, complex ones overfit.
Entropy H = minus the sum of p log2 p.
Decision trees choose the split with the largest information gain.
Linear regression: minimise squared error; gradient descent updates w by minus alpha times the gradient.
Bagging averages models; boosting trains them in sequence.

items: ELI5. Learning from examples is spotting the pattern in practice questions. Memorising every answer is overfitting: it fails on the new exam. We test on questions we kept hidden.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why keep some data aside to test?

Give a program thousands of examples of house sizes and prices, and ask it to predict the price of a new house. This is supervised learning. The hypothesis is a function; the learning algorithm searches for one that matches the examples.

A model that matches the training data perfectly is not necessarily good. A very flexible curve can wiggle through every point, including the noise, and predict poorly on a new house. This is overfitting.
To detect it, keep some data aside for testing, or use cross-validation, which rotates which part is held out.

A decision tree asks a series of questions. To choose the question, we measure how much it reduces uncertainty. Entropy measures uncertainty: zero when all examples agree, one bit for an even split between two classes. The best question is the one with the highest information gain.

Linear regression fits a line. We pick the weights that minimise the sum of squared errors. For one input there are closed forms. In general we use gradient descent: move the weights a small step against the gradient of the error. The step size is the learning rate.

Other models include nearest neighbours, which predict from the closest training examples, and support vector machines, which find a wide margin and use kernels for curved boundaries. Regularisation adds a penalty on weights to resist overfitting.
Ensembles, such as random forests and boosted trees, combine many weak models and often win on tabular data.

quiz.q: What is overfitting?
options: Fitting noise so new data are predicted poorly
Using too little data to test
quiz.explain: Training error is low, test error high.

quiz.q: What does entropy measure?
quiz.explain: Zero when the outcome is certain.

practice.title: Nearest neighbour
practice.intro: Write knn(train, labels, q, k): train is a list of numeric points (lists); labels the class of each; return the majority label among the k points closest (squared Euclidean distance) to q. Break ties in votes by choosing the label whose nearest member is closer.

practice.title: Gradient step
practice.intro: Write gd_line(xs, ys, w, b, lr, steps): fit y = w x + b by gradient descent on mean squared error, starting from w and b, for the given number of steps. Return [w, b] rounded to 6 decimals.
practice.solution:
def gd_line(xs, ys, w, b, lr, steps):
    n = len(xs)
    for _ in range(steps):
        gw = 0.0
        gb = 0.0
        for x, y in zip(xs, ys):
            e = w * x + b - y
            gw += 2 * e * x / n
            gb += 2 * e / n
        w -= lr * gw
        b -= lr * gb
    return [round(w, 6), round(b, 6)]

chapters.title: Neural networks and reinforcement learning

maps.title: Deep learning
links: Neuron | computes | Weighted sum plus activation

summary: Neural networks stack layers of simple units. Each unit takes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a nonlinearity such as ReLU. Back-propagation applies the chain rule backward to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.

Convolutional networks suit images, sharing small filters across positions. Transformers use attention and power modern language models. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards, not labelled answers: Q-learning estimates the value of each action in each state by temporal-difference updates.
The labs write a small forward pass, a softmax and a Q-learning update.

glossary.def: A nonlinearity such as ReLU or sigmoid.
Chain-rule gradient computation, output to input.
A small filter slid over an image.
A weighted focus on relevant inputs.
A scalar signal of how well the agent is doing.
The expected return of taking an action in a state.

keyPoints: A unit: output = activation(w . x + b).
Without nonlinear activations, many layers collapse into one linear map.
Training: forward pass, loss, back-propagation, weight update.
Regularisers: dropout, weight decay, data augmentation.
Q-learning: Q(s,a) += alpha (r + gamma max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)).
Explore with epsilon-greedy; exploit by taking the best known action.

items: ELI5. A neural network is a stack of tiny adjustable dials. Training turns the dials a little each time to reduce mistakes. Reinforcement learning is the same idea driven by rewards, like training a dog.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does one training step do to the dials?

A neuron takes numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them and a bias, and passes the sum through a nonlinear function. One neuron can draw a line between two classes. Many layers can draw complex shapes, because the nonlinearity prevents the layers from collapsing into a single linear map.

Training adjusts the weights to reduce a loss. The forward pass computes the output and the loss. Back-propagation uses the chain rule to find how the loss changes with each weight, working from the output back to the input. A gradient step then nudges all weights.
Doing this on mini-batches is stochastic gradient descent.

Special architectures use structure. A convolutional network slides small filters over an image, so it detects an edge anywhere with the same weights. Recurrent networks and especially transformers handle sequences.
A transformer lets every position attend to every other, weighing how relevant each is.

Reinforcement learning has no teacher with correct answers. The agent acts, receives rewards and learns what works. Its objective is the total discounted reward. It must balance exploring new actions with exploiting what it knows.
A simple rule, epsilon-greedy, takes a random action with small probability.

Q-learning applies this update after each step. The bracket is the temporal-difference error: the gap between what we just observed plus the best estimate afterwards, and what we predicted. Deep Q-networks use a neural network in place of a table.
Policy-gradient methods adjust a policy directly, and human feedback can train the reward itself.

options: Gradients of the loss for each weight

chapters.title: Language, perception, robots and the future of AI

maps.title: Applied AI
links: Language model | predicts | The next word
Robot planning | works in | Configuration space

summary: Natural language processing starts with language models: probability distributions over word sequences. Simple n-gram models count short sequences. Neural models trained on huge text collections now generate fluent text, though they can still state falsehoods confidently.

Computer vision recovers scene properties from images, using edges, motion, stereo and, above all, deep networks for recognition. Robots perceive, plan in a space of joint configurations, and control motors with feedback.
AI also raises questions about fairness, privacy, safety and control. The textbook's closing view is that machines should be uncertain about human preferences, so they stay open to correction.

glossary.def: A probability distribution over text.
A model that predicts a word from the previous n minus one words.
How surprised a model is by test text; lower is better.
Intersection over union of two boxes.
One axis per joint of the robot.
Making a machine's goals match human values.

keyPoints: Smoothing stops unseen n-grams getting zero probability.
Parsing assigns a grammatical structure; ambiguity is the main difficulty.
Image classification, detection and segmentation use convolutional or transformer networks.
Depth from stereo = focal length times baseline divided by disparity.
Motion planning in configuration space; controllers such as PID close the loop.
Fairness definitions can conflict when base rates differ.

items: ELI5. Language models guess the next word after reading a lot. Robots and cameras turn the physical world into numbers. All of it needs care: what we ask the machine to want matters a lot.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why should a machine be unsure about what people really want?

A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of words. The simplest kind, the bigram model, estimates the chance of each word given the previous one by counting in a large text. Unseen pairs would get probability zero, so we smooth the counts.

Modern models use embeddings, vectors that place similar words near each other, and a transformer with attention. They are pretrained on vast text to predict the next token, then adapted for tasks. They are fluent but can hallucinate: say things that sound right and are not supported.

Vision asks what is in an image. Edges are places where brightness changes sharply. Two cameras give depth: nearby points shift more between the images, so depth equals focal length times baseline over disparity.
Deep networks classify images, detect objects with boxes scored by intersection over union, and segment pixels.

A robot arm with many joints moves in a high-dimensional configuration space, where each point fixes all joint angles. Planners such as probabilistic roadmaps and rapidly exploring random trees sample this space and connect free points.
Controllers such as a PID loop use the error, its integral and its derivative to follow the plan. Robots also localise with particle filters and build maps at the same time, called SLAM.

Capable AI raises real concerns. Systems can be unfair if trained on biased data, and different fairness criteria cannot all hold when groups differ in base rates. Privacy, security and misuse matter. Safety means building systems that pursue what people truly want, not only what we wrote down.

The textbook closes with a proposal: build machines that are uncertain about human preferences and learn them from our behaviour. Such a machine has a reason to ask, to defer, and to allow itself to be switched off. The field's future depends on technical progress and on wise governance.
